author:

Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) asks whether the genes of a defined set (a pathway, a signature) cluster towards one end of a genome-wide ranked list \[1\]. Its canonical figure is the **running-score plot**: the ranked statistic as a bar code (top), the walking enrichment score that rises at set-member hits and falls at misses, peaking at the *enrichment score* (middle), and the set membership as a rug (bottom). Unlike over-representation analysis, GSEA uses the full ranked list — no arbitrary significance cutoff on the input genes — which is why the plot, not a table, carries the argument.

In R the analysis is handled by `clusterProfiler::GSEA()` \[2\] and the canonical figure by `enrichplot::gseaplot2()` \[3\]. This tutorial renders the canonical plot, stacks several gene sets on one ranked list, and then rebuilds the running score from primitives in ggplot2 so the statistic itself becomes legible. The Python counterpart of this tutorial is [GSEA Running-Score (Python)](../Python/GSEAPlot.html).

This tutorial covers seven workflows:

1. The canonical `gseaplot2` running-score plot with a p-value table;
2. Several gene sets overlaid on one ranked list;
3. A hand-built three-panel reconstruction of the running ES (ggplot2 + patchwork);
4. Comparing subtype-specific pathways across groups with a specificity heatmap;
5. An fgsea multi-pathway table plot (barcode rows + Size/NES/padj columns);
6. Redrawing Java-GSEA output as dot/barcode panels with aligned widths;
7. A radial pathway-gene hierarchy (ggraph) for enrichment results.

-   System Requirements: Cross-platform (Linux/MacOS/Windows)

-   Programming language: R

-   Dependent packages: `clusterProfiler`; `enrichplot`; `ggplot2`; `dplyr`; `patchwork`; `pheatmap`; `fgsea`; `ggraph`; `tidygraph`


## Data Preparation

To keep the tutorial fully reproducible we simulate the ranked list and the gene sets instead of downloading MSigDB: 2,000 genes ranked by a Wald-like statistic, a 60-gene "proliferation" set concentrated among the top ranks, a 50-gene "metabolic" set among the bottom ranks, and two neutral sets — the configuration that produces cleanly interpretable enrichment scores. `clusterProfiler::GSEA()` consumes a named, decreasing-sorted numeric vector (`geneList`) plus a `TERM2GENE` data frame.

```{r load data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(251)

n_genes <- 2000
genes <- paste0("Gene", sprintf("%04d", 1:n_genes))
stats <- rnorm(n_genes, sd = 2)
names(stats) <- genes

geneList <- sort(stats, decreasing = TRUE)   # must be decreasing-sorted

# Synthetic gene sets: one top-ranked, one bottom-ranked, two neutral
gs_up   <- genes[order(stats, decreasing = TRUE)[1:100]] |> sample(60)
gs_down <- genes[order(stats)[1:100]] |> sample(50)
gs_neu1 <- sample(genes, 80)
gs_neu2 <- sample(genes, 70)

term2gene <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(term = "Proliferation signature",     gene = gs_up),
  data.frame(term = "Metabolic repression",        gene = gs_down),
  data.frame(term = "Hypoxia response",            gene = gs_neu1),
  data.frame(term = "Immune checkpoint pathway",   gene = gs_neu2)
)

set.seed(251)  # GSEA permutes gene sets; keep p-values reproducible
gser <- GSEA(geneList, TERM2GENE = term2gene,
             minGSSize = 40, maxGSSize = 500,
             pvalueCutoff = 1,      # keep all sets for teaching
             eps = 0, seed = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)

as.data.frame(gser) |>
  dplyr::select(ID, setSize, enrichmentScore, NES, pvalue, p.adjust)
```

The negative NES of *Metabolic repression* marks a set enriched at the bottom of the list (down-regulated genes); the neutral sets hover around NES ≈ 0.

## Visualization

### 1. The Canonical Running-Score Plot

```{r}
#| label: fig-1.1GseaPlot2
#| fig-cap: "gseaplot2 of the top-ranked set: running enrichment score peaking at ES ≈ 0.98, hit rug, and ranked statistic; the inset table reports the permutation p-value."
#| out.width: "80%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| warning: false
#| message: false

gseaplot2(gser, geneSetID = 1, pvalue_table = TRUE,
          title = "Proliferation signature")
```

Three panels share one x-axis of rank positions: the running ES climbs steeply over the first 100 ranks (where the set members sit), peaks at the enrichment score, then decays; the rug marks the member positions; the bottom curve is the ranked statistic itself. The peak position defines the *leading edge* — the genes that drive the enrichment.

### 2. Several Gene Sets on One Ranked List

```{r}
#| label: fig-2.1GseaMulti
#| fig-cap: "Three gene sets overlaid on the same ranked list: a top-enriched set (positive NES), a bottom-enriched set (negative NES) and a neutral set."
#| out.width: "80%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| warning: false
#| message: false

ids <- match(c("Proliferation signature", "Metabolic repression", "Hypoxia response"),
             gser$ID)
gseaplot2(gser, geneSetID = ids, pvalue_table = FALSE,
          title = "Multiple gene sets on one ranked list")
```

Overlaying sets is how GSEA results are compared in practice: up-enriched sets peak early and plateau, down-enriched sets dive to a negative minimum near the end of the list, and null sets wander near zero. Legend labels follow the selected sets; the `color` argument controls the palette.

### 3. Rebuilding the Running Score from Primitives

```{r}
#| label: fig-3.1HandBuilt
#| fig-cap: "Hand-built three-panel running-score plot: the weighted Kolmogorov-Smirnov-like statistic is a running sum of ± steps at set members and misses."
#| out.width: "85%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| warning: false
#| message: false

in_set  <- names(geneList) %in% gs_up
w       <- abs(geneList)
step    <- ifelse(in_set, w / sum(w[in_set]), -1 / sum(!in_set))
run_es  <- cumsum(step)
peak    <- which.max(run_es)

df <- data.frame(rank = seq_along(geneList),
                 stat = as.numeric(geneList),
                 es = run_es, hit = in_set)

p_top <- ggplot(df, aes(rank, stat)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = rank, yend = 0, color = hit),
               linewidth = 0.15, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "#e63946")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#1d3557", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(y = "Ranked statistic", x = NULL) +
  theme_classic()

p_mid <- ggplot(df, aes(rank, es)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1d3557", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = df[peak, ], color = "#e63946", size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = peak, y = max(run_es), vjust = -0.8, hjust = 0,
           label = sprintf("ES = %.2f at rank %d", max(run_es), peak), size = 3.5) +
  labs(y = "Running ES", x = NULL) +
  theme_classic()

p_rug <- ggplot(df[df$hit, ], aes(x = rank, y = 1)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = rank, yend = 0.55),
               linewidth = 0.3, color = "#e63946") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void()

p3 <- p_top / p_mid / p_rug +
  plot_layout(heights = c(3, 2, 0.5))
p3
```

The weighted running ES is a cumulative sum: at each set member add its |statistic| normalized by the total member weight; at each miss subtract 1/(N − n). Rebuilding it from primitives demystifies `gseaplot2` — the shapes in Section 1 are exactly this walk — and makes custom variants (annotation of the leading edge, per-panel themes, multi-figure layouts) straightforward.

### 4. Comparing Subtype-Specific Pathways Across Groups

The running-score plot evaluates one ranked list at a time. In subtype (or cell-type) papers the recurring question is which pathways are **specific to each group** \[4\]. The workflow is: rank genes per group by one-vs-rest log2 fold change → run GSEA per group → collect each group's top pathways → display their activity in *all* groups as an unclustered heatmap, which makes the diagonal specificity pattern directly visible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-4.1SubtypeGsea
#| fig-cap: "Subtype-specific GSEA: the top-5 pathways of each simulated subtype show a diagonal specificity pattern."
#| out.width: "85%"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| warning: false
#| message: false

set.seed(251)
## Simulated expression matrix: 3 subtypes x 15 replicates x 1200 genes
genes   <- paste0("Gene", sprintf("%04d", 1:1200))
subtype <- rep(c("SubtypeA", "SubtypeB", "SubtypeC"), each = 15)
signal  <- matrix(0, nrow = length(genes), ncol = 3,
                  dimnames = list(genes, c("SubtypeA", "SubtypeB", "SubtypeC")))
pool <- genes
for (s in colnames(signal)) {          # 60 subtype-specific genes per subtype
  pick <- sample(pool, 60); signal[pick, s] <- 2; pool <- setdiff(pool, pick)
}
expr <- t(signal[, subtype]) +
  matrix(rnorm(length(subtype) * length(genes), sd = 0.6),
         nrow = length(subtype), ncol = length(genes))
colnames(expr) <- genes

## One-vs-rest log2FC per gene, per subtype (a t-test/limma loop can replace this)
lfc <- sapply(colnames(signal), function(s) {
  colMeans(expr[subtype == s, , drop = FALSE]) - colMeans(expr[subtype != s, , drop = FALSE])
})

## Signature gene sets: 5 sets of 30 genes per subtype
term2gene_sub <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(signal), function(s) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(k)
    data.frame(term = paste0(s, "_signature_", k),
               gene = sample(genes[signal[, s] > 0], 30))))
}))

## GSEA per subtype on its own ranked list
gsea_res <- lapply(colnames(signal), function(s) {
  GSEA(sort(lfc[, s], decreasing = TRUE), TERM2GENE = term2gene_sub,
       minGSSize = 10, maxGSSize = 100, pvalueCutoff = 1,
       eps = 0, seed = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
})
names(gsea_res) <- colnames(signal)

## Top-5 up-regulated pathways per subtype
top_gs <- lapply(gsea_res, function(r) {
  res <- as.data.frame(r)
  res <- res[res$NES > 0, ]
  head(rownames(res[order(res$NES, decreasing = TRUE), ]), 5)
})

## Specificity score: mean log2FC of each top set's genes in EVERY subtype
score <- t(sapply(unlist(top_gs, use.names = FALSE), function(gs) {
  gs_genes <- term2gene_sub$gene[term2gene_sub$term == gs]
  colMeans(lfc[gs_genes, , drop = FALSE])
}))
ann <- data.frame(Subtype = gsub("_signature_[0-9]+$", "", rownames(score)),
                  row.names = rownames(score))
jco <- c("#F2CCCC", "#E6D8CF", "#D5E3F0")
pheatmap(score, cluster_rows = FALSE, cluster_cols = FALSE,
         border_color = NA, annotation_row = ann,
         annotation_colors = list(Subtype = c(SubtypeA = jco[1], SubtypeB = jco[2],
                                              SubtypeC = jco[3])),
         main = "Subtype-specific top pathways")
```

The diagonal pattern confirms that each subtype's top pathways are indeed specific to it; a shared pathway would light up in several columns. The reference workflow \[4\] scores pathway activity with GSVA (`GSVA::gsva()`), which is the standard choice for real data — here we use the mean log2FC of each set's genes as a dependency-free approximation. For down-regulated pathways, take the top sets by ascending NES and sort rows accordingly.

::: callout-tip
## Practice tips

-   `geneList` must be a *named, decreasing-sorted* numeric vector, or `GSEA()` stops with "geneList should be a decreasing sorted vector".
-   Use `pvalueCutoff = 1` while exploring so filtered-out sets do not silently disappear from the result object.
-   Pass `seed = TRUE` (plus a `set.seed()` call) for reproducible permutation p-values.
-   Report NES with p.adjust, not the raw ES: ES depends on set size, NES is normalized for it.
:::

### 5. fgsea Multi-Pathway Table Plot

When many pathways must share one figure, `fgsea::plotGseaTable()` stacks them as **barcode rows** over a shared ranked list, with Size / NES / p / padj as aligned text columns on the right \[5\] — one glance carries the whole enrichment argument.

```{r}
#| label: fig-5.1FgseaTable
#| fig-cap: "fgsea table plot: eight hallmark-like pathways as barcode rows over one ranked list, statistics in the right-hand columns."
#| out.width: "95%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5

set.seed(401)
genes_f <- paste0("Gene", sprintf("%04d", 1:1500))
stats_f <- rnorm(1500, sd = 2)
names(stats_f) <- genes_f

## eight hallmark-like sets with graded enrichment (+ = up, - = down)
set_names <- c("MYC targets", "Cell cycle", "Inflammatory response", "Hypoxia",
               "Angiogenesis", "TGF-beta signaling", "EMT", "Wnt signaling")
enrich_amt <- c(2.5, 2, 1, 0.3, -0.3, -1, -2, -2.5)
pool <- genes_f
pathways_f <- lapply(seq_along(set_names), function(k) {
  hits <- sample(pool, 60)
  pool <<- setdiff(pool, hits)
  stats_f[hits] <<- stats_f[hits] + enrich_amt[k]
  hits
})
names(pathways_f) <- set_names
geneList_f <- sort(stats_f, decreasing = TRUE)

fgseaRes <- fgsea(pathways = pathways_f, stats = geneList_f,
                  minSize = 15, maxSize = 500, eps = 0)
fgseaRes <- fgseaRes[order(pval)]

plotGseaTable(pathways_f, geneList_f, fgseaRes, gseaParam = 0.5)

as.data.frame(fgseaRes)[, c("pathway", "size", "NES", "pval", "padj")]
```

::: callout-tip
## Practice tips

-   `fgsea()` accepts the same named, decreasing-sorted vector as `clusterProfiler::GSEA()`; `eps = 0` is the modern exact-mode setting (the old `nperm` argument is deprecated).
-   The table is sorted by p value, so the strongest signals sit at the top; feed a filtered result object to show only significant sets.
-   `gseaParam = 1` weights the running score by the statistic (the GSEA default); smaller values flatten the curve and make weak sets more visible.
:::

### 6. Redrawing Java-GSEA Output as Dot + Barcode Panels

Java-GSEA's per-pathway Excel only stores the running ES **at the genes inside the pathway** — that is why a line redraw never matches the official plot \[6\]. Dots at member positions are the faithful redraw; pairing them with a rank barcode beneath, and aligning the two panels' widths with `gridExtra`'s `unit.pmax()`, reproduces the paper look.

```{r}
#| label: fig-6.1JavaRedraw
#| fig-cap: "Java-GSEA output redrawn: running-ES dots at member positions (top) over a rank barcode (bottom), widths aligned with gridExtra."
#| out.width: "95%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

set.seed(402)
n_rank <- 2000
specs <- list(
  HALLMARK_MYC_TARGETS = list(idx = sort(sample(600, 110)),     dir =  1.0),
  HALLMARK_HYPOXIA     = list(idx = sort(sample(2000, 90)),     dir = -0.5),
  HALLMARK_EMT         = list(idx = sort(sample(1400:2000, 100)), dir = -1.0)
)
java_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(specs), function(pw) {
  spec <- specs[[pw]]
  hit <- seq_len(n_rank) %in% spec$idx
  step <- ifelse(hit, spec$dir / length(spec$idx), -spec$dir / (n_rank - sum(hit)))
  data.frame(pathway = pw,
             RANK.IN.GENE.LIST = seq_len(n_rank),
             RUNNING.ES = cumsum(step),
             member = hit)
}))

pal_j <- c(HALLMARK_MYC_TARGETS = "#E31A1C", HALLMARK_HYPOXIA = "#E7B800",
           HALLMARK_EMT = "#2E9FDF")

p_point <- ggplot(java_df, aes(RANK.IN.GENE.LIST, RUNNING.ES, fill = pathway)) +
  geom_point(data = subset(java_df, member), shape = 21, colour = "black",
             size = 1.6, stroke = 0.25) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal_j) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0),
                     limits = c(min(java_df$RUNNING.ES) - 0.02,
                                max(java_df$RUNNING.ES) + 0.02)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Enrichment score", fill = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.size = unit(3, "mm"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8))

p_rank <- ggplot(java_df, aes(RANK.IN.GENE.LIST, pathway, fill = pathway)) +
  geom_tile(data = subset(java_df, member), colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal_j) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Rank in gene list") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), panel.border = element_blank(),
        axis.line.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "none")

## stack the panels: patchwork equalises the shared x-axis widths automatically
p_point / p_rank + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(3, 1))
```

::: callout-tip
## Practice tips

-   Dots, not lines: the Java output's ES values exist only at member genes, so connecting them implies a curve that was never computed.
-   The original workflow equalised panel widths with `grid::unit.pmax()` over two `ggplotGtable()`s; `patchwork` (`p_point / p_rank + plot_layout(heights = ...)`) achieves the same shared-width, independent-height stacking and is the modern route.
-   Real inputs: read each pathway sheet with `read.delim()`, keep the `RANK.IN.GENE.LIST`, `RUNNING.ES` and `PROBE/NAME` columns, and rbind across pathways exactly as done here.
:::

### 7. Radial Pathway-Gene Hierarchy (ggraph)

Enrichment results have a natural hierarchy — pathways in the inner ring, their member genes outside — that the reference figure draws as **rings of bubbles around a centre** \[7\]: bubble size carries the gene's |fold change|, colour its direction. With tidygraph/ggraph the whole layout is one radial dendrogram, no bespoke ring maths needed:

```{r}
#| label: fig-7.1RadialHierarchy
#| fig-cap: "Radial pathway-gene hierarchy: pathways in the inner ring, member genes outside, bubble size = |logFC|, colour = direction."
#| out.width: "85%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7.5

set.seed(504)
pathway_defs <- list(
  "Cell cycle"        = c("CDK2", "CCNB1", "PCNA", "MCM2", "CDC20"),
  "p53 pathway"       = c("TP53", "MDM2", "CDKN1A", "BAX"),
  "DNA repair"        = c("BRCA1", "RAD51", "XRCC1", "PARP1", "ERCC1"),
  "EMT"               = c("VIM", "CDH1", "SNAI1", "TWIST1"),
  "Hypoxia"           = c("HIF1A", "VEGFA", "CA9", "EGLN3"),
  "Apoptosis"         = c("BCL2", "CASP3", "FAS", "XIAP")
)
gene_fc <- rnorm(length(unlist(pathway_defs)), sd = 1.6)
names(gene_fc) <- unlist(pathway_defs)

edges <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pathway_defs), function(pw) {
  data.frame(from = "Enrichment", to = pw)
}))
## gene node names must be unique across pathways: suffix with the pathway,
## keep the original gene name in a label column
edges <- rbind(edges, do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pathway_defs), function(pw) {
  data.frame(from = pw, to = paste0(pathway_defs[[pw]], "@", pw))
})))
nodes <- data.frame(
  name = c("Enrichment", names(pathway_defs),
           unique(unlist(lapply(names(pathway_defs), function(pw)
             paste0(pathway_defs[[pw]], "@", pw))))))
graph <- tidygraph::tbl_graph(nodes = nodes, edges = edges)

graph <- graph |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    is_gene = grepl("@", name),
    level   = ifelse(name == "Enrichment", 0, ifelse(is_gene, 2, 1)),
    label   = ifelse(is_gene, sub("@.*$", "", name), name),
    fc      = ifelse(is_gene, gene_fc[sub("@.*$", "", name)], NA_real_),
    leaf    = tidygraph::node_is_leaf())

ggraph(graph, layout = "dendrogram", circular = TRUE) +
  geom_edge_diagonal(colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_node_point(aes(filter = is_gene, size = abs(fc), colour = fc > 0),
                  alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_node_text(aes(filter = level == 1, label = label, angle = node_angle(x, y)),
                 size = 3.2, hjust = 0.5, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_node_text(aes(filter = is_gene, label = label,
                     x = x * 1.07,
                     angle = node_angle(x, y),
                     hjust = ifelse(x < 0, 1.08, -0.08)),   # by circle half, not by FC
                 size = 2.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#B2182B", `FALSE` = "#2166AC"),
                      labels = c("up", "down"), name = "logFC") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 5), name = "|logFC|") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        legend.key.size = unit(3, "mm"), legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 9))
```

::: callout-tip
## Practice tips

-   `layout = "dendrogram", circular = TRUE` is all the ring maths you need; `node_angle(x, y)` then rotates every label radially so text follows the ring.
-   Leaf labels with `hjust` on both sides of the circle keep gene names outside the outer ring instead of crossing it; inner-ring pathway names stay centred on their spokes.
-   Bubbles can only carry magnitude (|logFC|) — direction goes to colour. Deeper hierarchies (pathway → sub-pathway → gene) just extend the edge table.
:::

### 8. Pan-Cancer NES Bubble Grid Across Tumour Types

The pan-cancer companion of the running-score figure lays many tumour types side by side: for every tumour x pathway cell one bubble, colour carrying the normalized enrichment score (NES) and size its significance \[4\] - one glance answers which pathways move in which cancers. The simulated NES matrix below has a coherent pattern built in (proliferative cohorts move cell-cycle/p53, metabolic cohorts move hypoxia/glycolysis) so the reading order of the panel is verifiable; in a real pipeline the matrix comes from `fgsea::fGSEA()` on per-cohort limma contrasts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-8.1PanCancerNesGrid
#| fig-cap: "Pan-cancer NES bubble grid: tumour types across the base, pathways up the side; colour = normalized enrichment score, size = -log10(FDR); the built-in proliferation/metabolism pattern reads as designed."
#| out.width: "90%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 6.5

library(colorspace)
set.seed(7201)
tumors <- c("BLCA", "BRCA", "CESC", "CHOL", "COAD", "LUAD", "LUSC", "PAAD", "PRAD", "UCEC")
terms <- c("P53_PATHWAY", "CELL_CYCLE", "APOPTOSIS", "GLYCOLYSIS", "HYPOXIA",
           "EMT", "INFLAMMATION", "ANGIOGENESIS", "OXPHOS", "DNA_REPAIR")
nes <- matrix(rnorm(length(tumors) * length(terms), 0, 1.25),
              nrow = length(tumors), dimnames = list(tumors, terms))
# coherent biology: proliferative cohorts move cell-cycle/p53/DNA-repair up and
# apoptosis down; metabolic cohorts move hypoxia/glycolysis up
prolif <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)
metab  <- !prolif
for (k in seq_along(tumors)) {
  if (prolif[k]) { nes[k, c("CELL_CYCLE", "P53_PATHWAY", "DNA_REPAIR")] <-
                     nes[k, c("CELL_CYCLE", "P53_PATHWAY", "DNA_REPAIR")] + 1.7
                   nes[k, "APOPTOSIS"] <- nes[k, "APOPTOSIS"] - 1.4 }
  if (metab[k])  { nes[k, c("HYPOXIA", "GLYCOLYSIS")] <-
                     nes[k, c("HYPOXIA", "GLYCOLYSIS")] + 1.8 }
}
fdr <- matrix(10^(-(abs(as.numeric(nes)) * 0.9 + runif(length(nes), 0, 1.2))),
              nrow = length(tumors))
rownames(fdr) <- tumors; colnames(fdr) <- terms
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tumors, function(t)
  data.frame(tumor = t, term = colnames(nes), NES = nes[t, ], FDR = fdr[t, ],
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)))
stopifnot(sum(tab$FDR < 0.05 & abs(tab$NES) > 1.6) >= 12)
mypal <- colorRampPalette(c("#303B7F", "#EECA1F", "#D51113"))(n = 128)
p_b <- ggplot(tab, aes(tumor, term)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = -log10(FDR), colour = NES)) +
  scale_colour_gradientn("NES", colours = mypal, limits = c(-3, 3), na.value = "grey88") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.5, 6), guide = "none") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 9),
        axis.title = element_blank(), panel.border = element_rect(linewidth = 0.6),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
print(p_b)
```

::: callout-tip
**Practice tips**

-   Fix the colour scale with `limits = c(-3, 3)`: panels compared side by side must share one NES mapping or the comparison is void.
-   Size by `-log10(FDR)` and hide that legend - the reader should read colour (direction and strength), not fight two encodings at once.
-   Keep the non-significant cells visible via `na.value` instead of dropping them; the empty cross of cancers x pathways is itself information.
:::


### 9. Multi-Gene Single-Pathway Pan-Cancer Enrichment

The transpose of the NES grid above: one **pathway**, many genes. For a signature panel (here a ferroptosis gene list), GSEA is run per tumour type on the high-vs-low split of each gene, and the single pathway's NES fills a gene x tumour grid \[8\] - it answers at a glance in which cancers the panel's genes drive the pathway.

```{r gene-nes-ref, eval=FALSE}
# Reference workflow (real data): for every tumour x gene, rank by limma
# high-vs-low log2FC and run one fgsea::fGSEA() against the single GMT term;
# keep term/NES/pvalue/p.adj per cell -> the tab data frame below.
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-9.1GeneNesGrid
#| fig-cap: "Single-pathway pan-cancer NES grid with genes on the y-axis: ferroptosis-panel genes across ten tumour types, colour = NES, size = -log10(FDR); the planted first-half-up/second-half-down pattern reads as designed."
#| out.width: "95%"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 6

set.seed(1629)
tumors <- c("BLCA", "BRCA", "CESC", "CHOL", "COAD",
            "LUAD", "LUSC", "PAAD", "PRAD", "UCEC")
genes <- c("GPX4", "SLC7A11", "NFE2L2", "NCOA4", "ACSL4", "ALOX15", "FANCD2",
           "CISD1", "TP53", "HMOX1", "ATF4", "CHAC1", "SLC3A2", "GCLM")

## simulated single-pathway NES per gene x tumour (real pipeline: fgsea::fGSEA()
## on the per-cohort high-vs-low contrast of each gene's expression)
nes <- matrix(rnorm(10 * 14, 0, 1.1), 10, 14, dimnames = list(tumors, genes))
upg <- 1:7                                    # first-half panel moves EMT up
for (k in seq_along(tumors)) {
  nes[k, upg]  <- nes[k, upg] + 1.7
  nes[k, -upg] <- nes[k, -upg] - 1.5
}
fdr <- matrix(10^(-(abs(as.numeric(nes)) * 0.9 + runif(length(nes), 0, 1.1))), 10)
rownames(fdr) <- tumors; colnames(fdr) <- genes

tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(tumors, function(t)
  data.frame(tumor = t, gene = genes, NES = nes[t, ], FDR = fdr[t, ],
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)))
mypal <- colorRampPalette(c("#303B7F", "#EECA1F", "#D51113"))(n = 128)

ggplot(tab, aes(tumor, gene)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = -log10(FDR), colour = NES)) +
  scale_colour_gradientn("NES", colours = mypal, limits = c(-3, 3),
                          na.value = "grey88") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.5, 6), guide = "none") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 9),
        axis.title = element_blank(), panel.border = element_rect(linewidth = 0.6),
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "HALLMARK_EMT NES: ferroptosis genes x tumour types")
```

::: callout-tip
**Practice tips**

-   Which axis carries the genes is a design choice: genes-on-Y answers "which of *my* genes move this pathway where", pathways-on-Y answers "which pathway moves in this cohort" - fix it before choosing the aspect ratio.
-   One colour scale for the whole panel: the same `limits = c(-3, 3)` as the pathways-on-Y companion keeps the two grids directly comparable.
-   Pre-filter by `FDR` in the data, not by alpha in the theme; greyed-out non-significant cells (`na.value`) preserve the missing-data cross.
:::


## Application

Running-score GSEA plots are the standard figure for pathway-level interpretation of transcriptomic contrasts: tumor-vs-normal signatures, drug perturbation screens, and single-cell cluster markers. The panel below mirrors a typical publication layout: (A) the canonical single-set plot with p-value table and (B) the multi-set overlay.
